The history of cartography stretches from prehistoric sketches scratched into stone to the satellite-derived digital maps used by navigation software today. Early civilizations such as the Babylonians, Egyptians and Greeks produced maps that mixed practical surveying with cosmology. Ptolemy's Geography compiled coordinates for thousands of places and introduced systematic projections, while medieval portolan charts recorded compass bearings between harbors for Mediterranean sailors. The Age of Exploration demanded accurate charts of coastlines, and the Mercator projection of 1569 preserved angles so that lines of constant bearing appear straight, at the cost of exaggerating areas near the poles. Triangulation surveys in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, such as the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, measured baselines with chains and computed networks of triangles to fix positions with remarkable precision. Aerial photography, photogrammetry and finally GPS and remote sensing transformed mapmaking into a data science in which layers of information are stored in geographic information systems and rendered on demand.
